newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Japan, Portugal, Sweden among 5 new Council members.
newsitem.headline: Japan, Portugal, Sweden among 5 new Council members.

text.p: Costa Rica, Japan, Kenya, Portugal and Sweden were elected on Monday to the powerful 15-member U.N. Security Council for two-year terms beginning on January 1, 1997.
Four of the five seats were hotly contested. Only the election of Kenya, as the sole candidate for an African seat, was a foregone conclusion.

Japan, which will be serving its eighth term on the council, soundly beat India by 142 votes to 40 on the first round of ballotting for an Asian seat. A two-thirds majority of 120 votes, out of the 180 cast on that round, was needed for election to the council seat currently held by Indonesia.
Sweden and Portugal battered Australia in a three-cornered race for two seats reserved for the group called West European and Others, now filled by Germany and Italy.
Sweden was elected on the first ballot, with 153 votes, while Portugal obtained 112 and Australia 91. In a second round, Portugal received 124 votes to Australia's 57.
This will be only the second council term for Portugal -- it was a member in 1979-1980 -- and the third for Sweden, which served in 1957-58 and 1975-76.

The council's five permanent members, with the power of veto, are the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France. Five other non-permanent members whose two-year terms expire at the end of 1997 are: Chile, Egypt, Guinea-Bissau, Poland and South Korea.

The results of council elections are often highly predictable since regional groups usually nominate a single candidate for each vacancy, making the secret ballotting in the 185-member General Assembly a formality.

The Japan-India confrontation sparked particular interest, fuelled by speculation Japan was using its economic muscle to garner votes and that India, which has already served six turns on the council, might suffer because of its hold-out role in opposing a recently concluded Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty.

By contrast Australia, which has been on the Security Council four times, most recently in 1985-86, had been thought likely to benefit from its lead role in successfully shepherding the test ban treaty through the General Assembly last month. India's opposition to the treaty in the Geneva Disarmament Conference, which acts by consensus, helped block its adoption there.
In the race to fill a seat reserved for Latin American and Caribbean countries, Costa Rica, which has been a council member only once in 1974-75, romped home on the second ballot with 167 votes.

Its first round tally of 105 and rival Bolivia's 73 both failed to reach the required two-thirds majority. Bolivia then withdrew under a pre-election agreement, leaving the field clear for Costa Rica, current chairman of the so-called Group of 77 developing nations which now has 138 members, to win the council seat held until the end of December by Honduras.
Kenya, unopposed, received 172 votes on the first round and will succeed to an African seat filled now by Botswana. Kenya has served only once before on the council, in 1973-74.
A U.N. working group has been discussing enlarging and reforming the council for nearly three years. But while agreeing the council should be expanded, it has not yet decided how this should be done.

It is widely accepted that, if any new permanent seats are created, two of them should go to Germany and Japan in recognition of their status as economic superpowers and their increasing involvement in such areas as peacekeeping.
